source: Rudner (1953) The scientist qua scientist makes value judgments (as quoted in Uygun Tunc preprint 2025)
finding: Founding claim: no hypothesis is fully verified, so accepting one needs a decision that the evidence is strong enough, and how strong is a function of how bad a mistake would be. Read only through a 2025 secondary source, not the original.
numbers: No data. Philosophical argument.
quote: how strong is 'strong enough' is going to be a function of the importance, in the typically ethical sense, of making a mistake
limits: Original not opened. Rudner meant a rational reconstruction of the method, not a claim that scientists feel values (Dressel 2022 stresses this).
agent_relevance: Root of the rule: required confidence to accept a claim should scale with the cost of being wrong. The agent can set an accept threshold per claim from stated error costs.

source: Uygun Tunc (2025) Is the value-free ideal of science untenable? Part I: Inductive risk (preprint)
finding: Rebuilds the argument from inductive risk as two premises: epistemic insufficiency (internal standards cannot fix a threshold non-arbitrarily) and legitimate value-encroachment (social values may set it). Attacks both. Says it is an application of pragmatic encroachment from epistemology.
numbers: Preprint of about 11,335 words, draft dated 2025-04-21. No empirical data.
quote: the inductive risk argument does not pose a unique epistemic challenge beyond what is already implied by fallibilism
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Authors defend the value-free ideal, so this is one side of a live dispute.
agent_relevance: The cost-weighting premise is contested, not settled. Our agent should treat cost-scaled thresholds as a design choice, not a proven truth.

source: Uygun Tunc (2025) preprint, section on arbitrariness of thresholds
finding: Reply to the charge that thresholds like alpha 0.05 are arbitrary: fields pre-specify them and they differ with sample size and base rate of true hypotheses (5-sigma in particle physics versus 1.96-sigma elsewhere). Different cut-offs reflect error-rate calculations, so variation is evidence against arbitrariness. Also says a significance test accepts evidence, not a theory.
numbers: Examples given: alpha 0.05, alpha 0.00003, 5-sigma vs 1.96-sigma. No sample.
quote: the fact that different fields use different error thresholds testifies not for but against their arbitrariness
limits: Argument by reasoning. Contradicts the claim by Elliott (2022, cited there) that 90 or 99 percent would be equally good epistemically.
agent_relevance: Threshold can be anchored to checkable quantities (base rate, power, sample size) rather than to values. Prefer that anchor when it exists.

source: Uygun Tunc (2025) preprint, section on value-encroachment problems
finding: Lists costs of letting social values set thresholds: a meta-criterion problem (who picks the value-weighting rule), wishful thinking, category mistakes between belief and action, premature resolution of debates, and Mannheim-style paradoxes.
numbers: None.
quote: value-laden strategies would likely jeopardize the emergence of a rational consensus by prematurely resolving scientific debates
limits: Prediction by argument, no test. Dressel (b05) shows the Bayesian version avoids wishful thinking.
agent_relevance: Guard against one failure: error cost must change the action threshold, not the believed probability. Keep belief and decision separate (supports schema G5, code does the thresholding).

source: Dressel (2022) Inductive risk: does it really refute value-freedom? Theoria 37(2):181-207
finding: Models an ideal Bayesian agent that picks the action with highest expected utility. Threshold t is the probability where expected utility of acting equals that of not acting. Result: descriptively the perfect scientist need not make non-epistemic value judgements, so value-freedom is not refuted; normatively there are cases where she should use non-epistemic values, and this avoids wishful thinking and illegitimate prescription.
numbers: Binary decision, perform D iff p > t, with t where EU(perform) = EU(not perform). Outcomes split into first-order (truth, error, missed truth, averted error) and second-order.
limits: Idealised agent, single binary decisions, no sequences. Utility maximisation is not claimed to be the only rational rule.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact rule for the agent: act when p exceeds the break-even probability implied by the four outcome costs. This is code-checkable.

source: Hatchwell (2024) Individual values and inductive risk: remotivating the Bayesian alternative. Synthese 204:37
finding: Defends Jeffrey (1956): scientists should report probabilities, not accept or reject, which avoids inductive risk. Concedes that communication to policy may still be subject to the argument, and that choice of priors may smuggle in values. Notes the IPCC defence by Betz (2013) is criticised by Frank (2017) because choosing which probability statements to issue still involves inductive-risk judgements.
numbers: No data. 19-page journal article.
quote: the argument from inductive risk relies on faulty assumptions about the doxastic aims of science
limits: Her own text says second-order uncertainty (Rudner's regress) is the weightiest objection to the Jeffrey route. Steele (2012) also argues communicated probabilities still carry value choices.
agent_relevance: Rival to threshold-setting: keep a graded credence and let the downstream user pick the threshold. Our agent should output the probability plus the threshold used, so both views are served.

source: MacGillivray (2019) Null hypothesis testing is not scientific inference: a critique of the shaky premise of the science and values debate. Risk Analysis 39(7):1520-1532
finding: Argues the inductive risk argument is built on null hypothesis testing, a poor model of risk assessment. Proposes value-neutral inference with values handled in structured decision analysis. Notes regulators use cost-benefit reasoning in practice and cites the Delaney Clause as an absolutist threshold that became untenable.
numbers: Only figure: US agencies' benchmark upper-bound lifetime incremental cancer risk of 1e-6. Only the first 100,000 of 117,627 characters were read.
quote: null hypothesis testing, which I suggest is a poor descriptive and normative model for risk assessment
limits: Critique, not a test. The page was read through a summarising tool, last 17,627 characters unread.
agent_relevance: Move the cost weighing out of the evidence step and into an explicit decision step. This matches the schema split: model estimates, program decides.

source: Jeffrey (1956) Valuation and acceptance of scientific hypotheses; Levi (1960, 1962) (via Uygun Tunc 2025 and Hatchwell 2024)
finding: First replies to Rudner. Jeffrey: scientists assign probabilities and do not accept. Levi: separate accepting a hypothesis as true from acting on it. Rudner pre-empted Jeffrey with a second-order objection: the probability itself must be judged precise enough, and that judgement needs a threshold too.
numbers: None.
limits: Originals not opened. Known only through two 2024-2025 papers.
agent_relevance: The belief versus action separation is a long-standing rival to cost-shifted acceptance. Supports a two-slot output: credence, then action.

source: Kalai, Nachum, Vempala, Zhang (2025) Why language models hallucinate. arXiv 2509.04664
finding: Argues models guess because benchmarks score binary right or wrong. Proposes stating a confidence target t in the prompt: mistakes cost t/(1-t) points, correct answers 1, abstaining 0. This makes the Rudner threshold explicit and objective for grading.
numbers: t=0.5 gives penalty 1; t=0.75 penalty 2; t=0.9 penalty 9. Audit of 10 leaderboard evaluations: only WildBench gives minimal credit for saying I don't know. Pretraining bound: if 20% of facts appear once, base models hallucinate on at least 20% of them.
quote: Answer only if you are > t confident, since mistakes are penalized t/(1 - t) points
limits: A proposal plus theory. No experiment on whether models obey a stated t (see b10). Authors admit the chosen thresholds may be arbitrary.
agent_relevance: Direct formula for our agent: accept threshold t = cost_wrong / (cost_wrong + gain_right). Put t in the task prompt and in the code check.

source: Wang, Zhou, Devic, Fu (2026) Are LLM decisions faithful to verbal confidence? (RiskEval). arXiv 2601.07767
finding: Tests whether models change answer-or-abstain choices when the prompt states a larger penalty for wrong answers (scoring +1 correct, minus penalty wrong, 0 abstain). Models keep answering. They do not make cost-aware verbal confidence and do not adjust thresholds. Policy consistency with the optimal rule holds at low penalty then drops sharply, not smoothly. Utility goes strongly negative on hard sets.
numbers: Penalties 0 to 100 (grid 0,0.01,0.1,0.25,0.5,0.75,1,2,5,10,20,50,100). Datasets HLE, GPQA Diamond, GSM8K. Models include GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4.1-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2 (and Thinking), Qwen3-Next-80B, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 3 Flash, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemma-3n. HLE table averaged over penalty 10 or more: normalised utility -0.517 to -0.862 for the models in the first block; using the optimal policy on the model's own confidence raises it by about +0.31 to +0.69.
quote: models are neither cost-aware when articulating their verbal confidence, nor strategically responsive
limits: Single prompt framing; abstract says an instruction to use confidence changed little. Zero-shot only, no tool or code gate. Preprint (v1).
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that stating the cost in the prompt does not move a model's threshold. The agent must apply the threshold in code on extracted confidence, not ask the model to be careful.

source: RiskEval (Wang et al. 2026), calibration versus decision gap
finding: Confidence information is present but unused: applying the best threshold rule to the model's own stated confidence recovers much of the lost utility. So the failure is in the decision step, not the uncertainty estimate.
numbers: HLE high-penalty regime, normalised utility without and with the optimal policy: GPT-4.1-mini -0.537 to -0.087 (+0.450); Llama-4-Maverick -0.688 to -0.004 (+0.685); DeepSeek-V3.2 -0.853 to -0.169 (+0.683); Qwen3-Next-Think -0.862 to -0.295 (+0.567); GPT-5-mini -0.517 to -0.169 (+0.347).
limits: Gain computed under the model's stated belief, not true correctness, so it assumes the stated confidence is usable. HLE calibration error is high, so real gain would be smaller.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-side abstain rule on confidence. Calibrate the confidence first, since raw confidence is overconfident.

source: Wu et al. (2026) BAS: a decision-theoretic approach to evaluating LLM confidence. arXiv 2604.03216
finding: Metric that scores confidence by realised utility across a range of risk thresholds t, with an asymmetric penalty on overconfident errors. Frontier models stay overconfident. Models with similar ECE or AURC can have very different BAS. Simple fixes help: top-k confidence elicitation and post-hoc calibration.
numbers: 12 models, SimpleQA, MedQA, AIME. SimpleQA ECE ranges 49.0% to 84.2%, all models negative BAS. AIME: GPT-4o 11.7% accuracy with BAS -5.06; GPT-oss 75.0% with BAS 0.57. Isotonic calibration on SimpleQA: Llama-3.3-70B BAS -2.97 to 0.02; GPT-4o-mini -3.86 to 0.001; ECE drops from 60-90% to low single digits.
quote: even frontier models remain prone to severe overconfidence
limits: Self-reported confidence only. Uniform prior over risk thresholds by default. Calibration needs a validation set from the same task. Preprint under review.
agent_relevance: Calibrate confidence on held-out items before applying a cost threshold. Report BAS-like utility, not just accuracy, when testing the agent.

source: Jurayj, Cheng, Van Durme (2025) Is that your final answer? Test-time scaling improves selective question answering. arXiv 2502.13962
finding: More reasoning compute raises confidence in correct answers, so a fixed confidence threshold lets the model answer more questions correctly. Defines three cost settings: Exam Odds (no penalty), Jeopardy Odds (wrong costs the same as right gains), High-Stakes Odds (wrong costs much more). Under Exam Odds the best threshold is 0; under Jeopardy Odds a threshold of 0.95 lifts utility strongly. Models that tie at Exam Odds can differ at Jeopardy Odds.
numbers: DeepSeek R1-32B and s1-32B on AIME-style 3-digit-answer tasks, token budgets up to several thousand; threshold 0.95 used for Jeopardy. Authors say 0.95 is not claimed optimal.
limits: Two open models only, confidence is from the model's own answer-token probability. Exact scores are in figures, not read as numbers. The authors warn a threshold may not be the right calibration approach.
agent_relevance: Rankings change with the cost setting. Evaluate the agent at more than one error-cost ratio. More thinking before deciding raises the confidence signal.

source: Zollo et al. (2024) Prompt Risk Control. ICLR 2024, arXiv 2311.13628
finding: Picks the prompt by a statistical upper bound on a risk measure (for example worst-case or CVaR) rather than average reward. In the chatbot test, the prompt chosen for best average reward broke the toxicity risk limit on held-out data, while the PRC prompt kept it below the limit.
numbers: Anthropic HH data, Flan-T5-XXL, 20 candidate prompts, 3500 validation points. Goal: toxicity loss at the 0.925 quantile not above 0.05 with 95% probability (delta 0.05).
quote: Prompt selection according to the best reward leads to an unacceptably high VaR
limits: The risk level is set by the user, so the value judgment is moved, not removed. Needs validation data and assumes deployment looks like it.
agent_relevance: A tested way to turn a stated error tolerance into a code-chosen setting with a guarantee. Shows choosing by average hides the worst cases.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Conformal Thinking: risk control for reasoning on a compute budget. ICML 2026, arXiv 2602.03814
finding: Turns the stopping threshold into a user-stated error rate. An upper confidence threshold stops when the model is confident (risk: wrong answer); a lower threshold stops unsolvable items early (risk: giving up on a solvable one). Distribution-free risk control keeps test risk under the target. The lower threshold saves tokens most when many items are unsolvable.
numbers: Models Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, Qwen3-VL-8B. Data: AIME 1983-2025 (1011 samples), DeepScaleR subset (1189), GPQA-Diamond (198), MathVision. Solvable:unsolvable ratios 3:1, 1:1, 1:3 tested.
limits: Validation set must resemble test set; the paper tests math to science shift. Token-count signal does not hold the target under shift. Hard-to-structure reasoning tasks lack good signals.
agent_relevance: Two kinds of error get two thresholds. Maps to the agent: a doubt/stop rule for false-confident stops and a give-up rule for false-negative stops, each tied to a stated tolerance.

source: Einbinder, Davidov, Teh, Gal, Romano (2026) Selective Safety Steering via Value-Filtered Decoding. arXiv 2605.14746
finding: Filters tokens by a value-based safety score and a threshold that directly sets the rate of unnecessary interventions (type-I error). One threshold trades output safety against fidelity to the base model. Beats baselines on safety, helpfulness and similarity trade-offs.
numbers: Datasets HH-RLHF, BeaverTails, PKU-SafeRLHF; thresholds 0.45, 0.85, 0.65 respectively; value estimator trained on 5,000 prompts with 24 (HH-RLHF) or 16 samples each; calibration sets about 86%, 79%, 86% safe completions.
quote: This gives the threshold a precise statistical interpretation: it directly controls the type-I error
limits: Safety-steering setting, not claim acceptance. On unsafe outputs it is only comparable to baselines. Tuned threshold differs per dataset.
agent_relevance: Shows a cost threshold can be a calibrated, auditable dial with a stated false-alarm rate, rather than a prompt instruction.

source: Shen and Kejriwal (2023) A formalism and approach for improving robustness of LLMs using risk-adjusted confidence scores. arXiv 2310.03283
finding: Defines decision risk (answering too aggressively) and composite risk (including unanswerable or ambiguous items) for NLI. Their DwD method re-adjusts raw confidence and lets the model skip risky items. With ChatGPT it answers an extra 20.1% of low-risk items it wrongly judged high-risk and skips a further 19.8% of high-risk items it would have got wrong.
numbers: 4 NLI benchmarks, 3 baselines, RoBERTa and ChatGPT. RoBERTa: in-domain and out-of-domain decision risk cut by margins of 28.3% and 18.9%. ChatGPT composite risk cut a further 17.9% over next best baseline. Reductions significant at 95% confidence.
limits: NLI only, risk injected by synthetic functions that emulate unanswerable items. Older models. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that a learned risk adjustment to confidence beats raw confidence both ways: fewer wrong answers and fewer needless refusals.

source: Kalai et al. (2025) audit of benchmarks (Why language models hallucinate, Table 2 and appendix F)
finding: Mainstream evaluations (GPQA, MMLU-Pro, SWE-bench, HLE, IFEval and others) give zero credit for I don't know, so a model that always guesses beats one that abstains. This builds the no-cost-for-error threshold into training and ranking. Notes that LLM judges can wrongly accept long incorrect answers.
numbers: 10 evaluations audited; 1 gives minimal abstention credit; two curated leaderboards overlap by 50%. HELM Capabilities: 4 of 5 scenarios give no credit for IDK.
limits: Audit of grading rules from reading benchmark documents, not a measured effect on model behaviour. OpenAI-authored.
agent_relevance: Explains b10: models are tuned at threshold zero. The agent's own tests must use scoring with an explicit penalty or it will drift to guessing.

source: Dressel (2022), scope conditions and open questions in Rudner's classic answer
finding: Key moderator: the argument only bites in an applied decision where consequences reach beyond science. Rudner's frequentist framing leaves open how consequences determine t, how scientific and extra-scientific outcomes combine, and how the chance of error maps to the chance of harm. The Bayesian model answers these by summing expected utilities.
numbers: None. Footnote scope limits: individual decisions, binary choices, single methodological items.
limits: Does not model sequences of decisions or three-way accept, reject, suspend choices, though says it could.
agent_relevance: Cost weighting matters when the answer feeds an action. For pure belief questions with no use, the agent can stay at a default threshold.

source: Uygun Tunc (2025) on scope limits and rival responses (Jeffrey, Betz, Levi, Lacey, Steele, Stegenga)
finding: Lists the moderators in the literature: the argument concerns cases with foreseeable practical consequences and where withholding judgment or deferral is undesirable. Scope is then policy advice (Steele 2012) and possibly fast science (Stegenga 2024). Responses include rejecting acceptance (Jeffrey), conditionalising claims (Betz 2013), separating accepting from acting (Levi), and splitting acceptance into endorsing, adopting, holding (Lacey 2015).
numbers: None.
limits: Citation map only. The cited works were not opened by this agent.
agent_relevance: When abstaining or deferring is cheap, cost-shifted thresholds matter less. Give the agent an explicit defer option and test whether it is used.

source: Elliott (2022) via Uygun Tunc: thresholds could equally be 90 or 99 percent
finding: The pro-argument claim that purely epistemic standards do not choose between a 90, 95 or 99 percent significance level. Seen only as a quote inside the 2025 preprint.
numbers: 90, 95, 99 percent significance levels. No data.
limits: Original not opened; the rival claim in b03 says field-specific error calculations do choose.
agent_relevance: No evidence that any one threshold is correct. Supports choosing thresholds from error costs plus base rates, not a fixed universal number.

source: Steele (2012) The scientist qua policy advisor makes value judgments; Betz (2013); Frank (2017) (via Hatchwell 2024)
finding: Test case for the Jeffrey route: the IPCC reports probabilities. Betz says this evades inductive risk. Frank (2017) and Steele (2012) reply that choosing which probabilities and how to calibrate the verbal likelihood scale still involves value judgments.
numbers: None.
limits: Seen through Hatchwell 2024, originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Even reporting a probability hides a threshold (which statements to issue, which confidence labels to use). The agent should log how it maps numbers to words.

source: Hatchwell (2024), cognitive load and prior-choice objections
finding: Two named objections to the credence-only route are examined: it is too demanding for limited agents (cognitive load argument), and priors themselves embed values. She answers both but grants that communication may remain subject to the argument.
numbers: None.
limits: Philosophical reply, no data.
agent_relevance: A graded-credence agent needs priors. Show priors as explicit parameters so they can be audited.

source: Gap statement: no human behavioural data found on scientists' thresholds under varying error costs
finding: The only experiment found that varies stated error cost and measures the decision against the break-even point is the RiskEval design, in machines. The philosophical papers read reason about thresholds and report no data on what scientists actually do. This is a gap, not a finding of no studies.
numbers: No study found in the sources read.
limits: Absence reported from limited searching. The arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate limited this session, and only 4 of 6 allowed web searches were used by this agent. Such data could exist in sociology or psychology of science.
agent_relevance: The agent design cannot lean on human replication data. It should test its own thresholds with penalty-sweep experiments like b10.

source: Wang et al. (2026) RiskEval, failure shape across penalty sizes
finding: Failure is not a smooth under-reaction. Policy consistency is high at low penalty (about 5 or less) then drops abruptly (about 10 or more). So models have no penalty-dependent threshold; they hold an answer-by-default habit that persists until the penalty is large.
numbers: Policy consistency high for penalty at most 5, then abrupt drop at 10 or more, on HLE and GPQA Diamond. Mean normalised regret rises almost monotonically with penalty.
limits: Read from figure text and captions, not raw tables. GSM8K is easy so tests little.
agent_relevance: Do not trust prompt-stated penalties at any size. Test the agent at penalties of 1, 10 and 100.

source: Jurayj et al. (2025), selective QA recipe and related game-show work
finding: Recommends reporting both Exam Odds and Jeopardy Odds results. Reports that R1-32B scales better than s1-32B at larger budgets under the stricter setting, a gap invisible in accuracy alone. Notes game-show systems already used penalties to force abstention.
numbers: Confidence threshold 0.95 for Jeopardy Odds; appendix adds a High-Stakes Odds setting and a second dataset with token budgets 500 to 4000.
limits: Only two models; no human comparison.
agent_relevance: A benchmark protocol to adopt: report utility at several penalty ratios.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Conformal Thinking, validity under distribution shift
finding: Guarantees hold when validation and test match. Under shift between math and science, risk stays below target for confidence and probe signals but not for the token-count signal; lower-threshold risk shows less robustness to length change.
numbers: Validation on AIME to test on GPQA-Diamond and the reverse. Validation-set size study with fixed test size 800 on Qwen3-8B with DeepScaleR.
limits: Exact violation counts not extracted. Based on figure captions and nearby prose.
agent_relevance: A cost threshold learned on one domain may not carry to another. Recalibrate per domain.
